Question: Could the CrowdStrike software problem have been handled by doing a Safe Mode boot of the effected systems so the Falcon software would not attempt a load? Or is that not Possible with Windows Enterprise systems?
Answer: Yes. You can boot it in Safe Mode, and if it disallows that, then WRE (Windows Recovery Environment). Then you delete all files matching the pattern:       C:\Windows\System32\drivers\CrowdStrike\C-00000291*.sys And reboot. As I stated previously, this is really easy to automate in a scripted PXE boot environment, which also means remotely, assuming you have remote power cycle capability for the servers in your datacenter.

Question: As a function of a qubit's realizable states and their complex states in and out of superposition, would it ever be possible to have quadrabits, pentabits, etc, which possess the unrealized phase states of a qubit beyond 2 degreees of freedom?
Answer: The binary value is a fiction. It’s based on the amplitude of the wave at the time of the measurement, and therefore collapse of the wave. Technically, until that happens, the value is effectively analog. It could in fact represent a transcendental number, without end.

Question: Since 2014, with the acquisition of WhatsApp, Instagram, Oculus, Giphy, etc and all monetary losses inclusive, is Mark Zuckerberg making good business decisions?
Answer: The WhatsApp purchase was a leverage purchase, to force third world phone companies to allow Zuckerberg to provide Internet service, including Facebook, to people in third world countries with no Internet access. He bought the company for $18B, which was a steal, at $9B/year SMS revenue taken in by the companies he wanted to threaten to take away their SMS revenue, if they did not let him have his way. It was a resounding success. Internet ORG is available to Airtel customers in Ghana, Kenya and Zambia, Tigo customers in Colombia and Tanzania, and Reliance customers in India, with more countries planned. I haven’t really followed Instagram. I think Zoom stole all the available thunder from Oculus, other than for gamers. Giphy, etc., I never really had an interest in, although the search capability on Giphy implies technology that perhaps Zuckerberg wanted for Facebook.

Question: In what ways can the stability of a DMDR token reduce investment risks and enhance profitability?
Answer: It can’t. In theory — and if this were in fact true, they’s be listed on a cryptocurrency exchange somewhere, and they’re not — they are backed by a 1 carat lab grown diamond. That’s 0.2 grams. The problem with lab grown diamond is that it’s not a commodity to back a currency; unlike silver or gold, you can create lab diamonds all day long, from soot or charcoal, It’s like being able to print dollars; if you could do that, they would be worthless. Despite what’s charged for cut lab grown diamonds, the DMDR token is nowhere near that value, even with a complex cut applied, and the DMDR tokens which are backed by these things are backed by uncut lab grown diamonds, so there is not even a (greatly inflated) labor value add to the cost. You want you lab grown diamond? Here, let me grow one for you; it’ll be a few weeks, because we use the HPHT method, and it takes 2 weeks to grow 1 carat; we’re not stupid, though, so we never grow them only one at a time. Bulk production further reduces our production costs (and the value of your token, if you cash out to diamonds). So the risk is still there, with the added bonus that no exchange is willing to list them.

Question: How does the performance and security of open source Darwin compare to mainstream Linux, BSD, and other Unix systems?
Answer: Darwin is essentially macOS, without the proprietary optimizations licensed from other sources, and sits as an integrated BSD “Single Server” on top of OSF/Mach. There are certain aspects of this arrangement which lead to lower performance — the math libraries, especially, are lower performance than the licensed libraries you can’t have. The additional boundary layering can also cost performance. As can certain features, such as membership of a given user credential or filesystem or other credentialed object in an essentially unlimited number of groups. However, Darwin is extremely secure, much more than Linux or BSD, because of the way that the user/kernel boundary crossing credential enforcement is handled. Note: I wrote almost all of that code But realize that there are also things about Darwin that are not covered via the same security capabilities in specialty versions of BSD or Linux, such as seLinux, or seBSD — particularly now that the MACF framework and loading of kernel modules in macOS has been deprecated. So, for example, there are a number of NSA security modules you can no longer load into macOS, and therefore Darwin, that you can load in those Linux and BSD variants, such as FLASK and TE: You should really get out more, and read more security related CS research papers. You also need to be aware that instead of dealing with Darwin, you can simply download the macOS source code from Apple, and use that instead. Most people don’t use Darwin directly because of this. But if you want a particular example, if you look at the SUGID code in Darwin/macOS, abd compare it with that in Linux and BSD variants, you will likely see a group membership hole you could drive a truck through, as a security bug in both of them. Particularly as regards “exclusion groups”, which is about as big a hint as I am willing to get. You will also see in the group enforcement code a reversal of the order of group/world checking, which is a performance enhancement on which I have a pending patent of mine, assigned to Apple.
